newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina hopes for U.S. beef access by January.
newsitem.headline: Argentina hopes for U.S. beef access by January.

text.p: Argentina hopes to have final approval for beef exports to the United States by January, a the top Argentine trade officials said Wednesday.
Argentine authorities are annoyed by what they regard as slow progress by the U.S. Department of Agriculture in granting sanitary approval for an agreed 20,000-tonne quota.

"We are very firm in demanding that this is an agreement within the framework of GATT and we that have to have access, and we hope that we are going to have it from January," said Secretary for International Economic Relations Jorge Campbell.
Asked whether Argentina would complain to the World Trade Organization about the matter, Campbell told reporters: "We are still waiting and we are still not analyzing a dispute of that sort."

Campbell said Argentina hoped for a positive verdict soon from a South Korean sanitary mission to authorize beef exports to that country. Argentina has accused South Korea and Japan of using sanitary rules as an excuse to keep its beef out.
Argentine beef was for decades excluded from major markets because of problems with foot and mouth disease, but its herd of 50 million has now gone for more than two years without an outbreak.
Visiting WTO chief Renato Ruggiero said that Argentine officials had brought up the beef issue with him.

"There have been some comments about the difficulties that they find in their exports, without mentioning one country or the other but mentioning phitosanitary problems that they meet," Ruggiero said.

"And I said that there are very clear procedures of the WTO that you can use to defend your interests and so I invited them, more than complaining, to try and define the best way to defend their interests," he also told reporters.

Argentine beef producers said they feared delays in U.S. sanitary approval could slow down the process of opening up vital markets in Asia. Argentina has already gained access to a number of the region's markets including the Phillippines, Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong, but the juiciest markets, Japan and South Korea, have proved harder to prise open.
The Argentine government has set itself a target of reaching exports of a million tonnes a year of beef by 2000, although many in the industry think this overly optimistic.
Exports surged by 36 percent to 510,000 tonnes last year, but have since slackened off, partly due to the effects on European demand of the "mad cow" scare.
